amc12-ahsme-1979-01.title: Half of each side
amc12-ahsme-1979-01.body:
$DE=\frac12AD$ and $DG=\frac12CD$, so the area of $DEFG$ is $\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14$ of $72$, which is $18$.

**Answer: (D) $18$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-01.title: Count pieces
amc12-ahsme-1979-01.body:
Lines through $E$ and $G$ parallel to the sides cut $ABCD$ into $4$ congruent rectangles, one of which is $DEFG$: $72\div4=18$.

**Answer: (D) $18$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-03.title: Isosceles triangle
amc12-ahsme-1979-03.body:
$AD=AB=AE$, so $\triangle ADE$ is isosceles with apex angle $\angle DAE=90^\circ+60^\circ=150^\circ$. Its base angles are $\frac{180^\circ-150^\circ}{2}=15^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) $15$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-03.title: Symmetry check
amc12-ahsme-1979-03.body:
By symmetry $\angle BEC=15^\circ$ too, and $\angle AED+\angle DEC+\angle CEB=60^\circ$ gives $\angle DEC=30^\circ$, consistent with the isosceles triangle $DEC$ having base angles $75^\circ$ ($=90^\circ-15^\circ$).

**Answer: (C) $15$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-04.title: Plug in $x=1$
amc12-ahsme-1979-04.body:
The expression is $1\cdot[1\cdot(1-4)+10]+1=8$. The choices give $16,12,4,-16,8$; only (E) gives $8$.

**Answer: (E) $-x^4+2x^3-4x^2+10x+1$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-05.title: Palindrome
amc12-ahsme-1979-05.body:
The number reads the same with first and last digits swapped, so it is $\overline{aba}$. It is even, so $a$ is even; the largest choice is $a=8$, $b=9$: $898$. Digit sum $8+9+8=25$.

**Answer: (D) $25$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-06.title: Split off the 1s
amc12-ahsme-1979-06.body:
Each fraction is $1+\frac1{2^k}$, so the sum is $6+\left(\frac12+\frac14+\dots+\frac1{64}\right)-7=6+\frac{63}{64}-7=-\frac1{64}$.

**Answer: (A) $-\frac{1}{64}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-07.title: Use the root
amc12-ahsme-1979-07.body:
If $x=n^2$ with $n=\sqrt x\ge0$, the next square is $(n+1)^2=n^2+2n+1=x+2\sqrt x+1$.

**Answer: (E) $x+2\sqrt{x}+1$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-07.title: Test
amc12-ahsme-1979-07.body:
$x=4$: next square $9=4+2\cdot2+1$. The other choices give $5,17,25,20$.

**Answer: (E) $x+2\sqrt{x}+1$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-08.title: Quarter circle
amc12-ahsme-1979-08.body:
The lines $y=x$ and $y=-x$ ($y\ge0$) make a right angle at the origin, cutting the disk of radius $2$ into a $90^\circ$ sector and a $270^\circ$ piece. The smaller is a quarter of the disk: $\frac14\cdot4\pi=\pi$.

**Answer: (C) $\pi$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-10.title: Midpoints on a circle
amc12-ahsme-1979-10.body:
The side midpoints lie on a circle of radius $2$ (the apothem), $60^\circ$ apart. $Q_1$ and $Q_4$ are diametrically opposite, so $Q_1Q_4=4$; $Q_2Q_3$ subtends $60^\circ$, so $Q_2Q_3=2$. The quadrilateral is an isosceles trapezoid with height $2\sin60^\circ=\sqrt3$. Area $=\frac{4+2}{2}\cdot\sqrt3=3\sqrt3$.

**Answer: (D) $3\sqrt{3}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-10.title: Triangles from the center
amc12-ahsme-1979-10.body:
Split into triangles $OQ_1Q_2$, $OQ_2Q_3$, $OQ_3Q_4$, each with two sides $2$ and angle $60^\circ$: area $\frac12\cdot2\cdot2\cdot\sin60^\circ=\sqrt3$ each. Total $3\sqrt3$.

**Answer: (D) $3\sqrt{3}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-12.title: Two isosceles triangles
amc12-ahsme-1979-12.body:
Let $\angle BAO=x$. Since $AB=OD=OB$, $\triangle ABO$ is isosceles and $\angle BOA=x$. The exterior angle gives $\angle EBO=2x$. Since $OB=OE$, $\angle BEO=2x$. Now $\angle EOD$ is an exterior angle of $\triangle AOE$: $\angle EOD=\angle OAE+\angle AEO=x+2x=3x=45^\circ$, so $x=15^\circ$.

**Answer: (B) $15^\circ$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-12.title: Arcs
amc12-ahsme-1979-12.body:
$\angle BAO$ is formed by two secants from $A$, so it equals half the difference of the intercepted arcs: $x=\frac{\stackrel\frown{ED}-\stackrel\frown{BC}}{2}=\frac{45^\circ-x}{2}$ (arc $BC$ equals $\angle BOC=x$). Then $3x=45^\circ$, $x=15^\circ$.

**Answer: (B) $15^\circ$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-13.title: Split by sign of $x$
amc12-ahsme-1979-13.body:
$\sqrt{x^2}=|x|$, so the inequality is $y<x+|x|$.
- If $x\ge0$: $y<2x$.
- If $x<0$: $y<0$.

Now check (A): if $x\ge0$ and $y<0$ then also $y<2x$; if $x<0$ and $y<2x$ then $y<0$. So “$y<0$ or $y<2x$” is exactly the solution set.

**Answer: (A) $y<0$ or $y<2x$ (or both inequalities hold)**

amc12-ahsme-1979-13.title: Rule out others
amc12-ahsme-1979-13.body:
- $(x,y)=(1,1)$ satisfies the inequality ($0<1$) but not (D).
- $(x,y)=(-1,-1)$ satisfies it ($0<1$) but not (E).
- $(x,y)=(1,-1)$ satisfies it ($-2<1$) but not (C) ($1<-2$ is false).
- $(x,y)=(-1,1)$ does not satisfy it ($2<1$ is false) but satisfies (B).

Only (A) remains.

**Answer: (A) $y<0$ or $y<2x$ (or both inequalities hold)**

amc12-ahsme-1979-14.title: Ratio of products
amc12-ahsme-1979-14.body:
The $n$-th number is $\frac{n^2}{(n-1)^2}$. So the third is $\frac94$ and the fifth $\frac{25}{16}$. Sum $\frac{36}{16}+\frac{25}{16}=\frac{61}{16}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{61}{16}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-15.title: Unit jars
amc12-ahsme-1979-15.body:
Let each jar hold $1$. The first has alcohol $\frac{p}{p+1}$ and water $\frac1{p+1}$; the second $\frac q{q+1}$ and $\frac1{q+1}$. Ratio:
$$\frac{\frac p{p+1}+\frac q{q+1}}{\frac1{p+1}+\frac1{q+1}}=\frac{p(q+1)+q(p+1)}{(q+1)+(p+1)}=\frac{p+q+2pq}{p+q+2}.$$

**Answer: (E) $\frac{p+q+2pq}{p+q+2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-15.title: Test values
amc12-ahsme-1979-15.body:
$p=1$, $q=3$: jars are half and three-quarters alcohol, so the mix is $\frac58$ alcohol, ratio $5:3$. (E): $\frac{1+3+6}{6}=\frac53$ ✓; (A) gives $2$, (B) $\frac52$, (C) $\frac32$, (D) $\frac{13}{6}$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{p+q+2pq}{p+q+2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-16.title: Ratio of areas
amc12-ahsme-1979-16.body:
The small circle is $\frac13$ of the big circle's area, so its radius is $\frac{3}{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3$.

**Answer: (E) $\sqrt{3}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-17.title: Triangle inequality
amc12-ahsme-1979-17.body:
The triangle has sides $AB=x$, $BC=y-x$, $CD=z-y$. The three strict triangle inequalities:
- $x<(y-x)+(z-y)=z-x$, i.e. $x<\frac z2$ (I).
- $y-x<x+(z-y)$, i.e. $y<x+\frac z2$ (II).
- $z-y<x+(y-x)=y$, i.e. $y>\frac z2$ — so III is never true.

I and II must hold.

**Answer: (C) I. and II. only**

amc12-ahsme-1979-17.title: Example
amc12-ahsme-1979-17.body:
$x=2$, $y=5$, $z=8$ gives sides $2,3,3$, a real triangle. Here $y=5>\frac z2=4$, so III fails while I and II hold.

**Answer: (C) I. and II. only**

amc12-ahsme-1979-18.title: Compare with $\frac{10}{7}$
amc12-ahsme-1979-18.body:
$\frac{10}{7}$ corresponds to $\log_{10}5=0.7$, very close to $0.699$; the neighbouring choices correspond to $\log_{10}5\approx0.778$ and $0.636$, far away.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{10}{7}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-19.title: Powers of 2
amc12-ahsme-1979-19.body:
$256^{32}=2^{256}$, so $x^{256}=2^{256}$. The real solutions are $x=\pm2$. Sum of squares $4+4=8$.

**Answer: (A) $8$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-20.title: Tangent addition
amc12-ahsme-1979-20.body:
$\frac32(b+1)=2$ gives $b=\frac13$. Then $\tan(\arctan a+\arctan b)=\frac{\frac12+\frac13}{1-\frac16}=1$, and the sum lies in $(0,\frac\pi2)$, so it is $\frac\pi4$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{\pi}{4}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-21.title: Area = rs
amc12-ahsme-1979-21.body:
The tangent lengths from the right-angle vertex are $r$, so the legs are $r+m$ and $r+n$ with $m+n=h$. The semiperimeter is $s=h+r$, and the area is $rs=r(h+r)$. The ratio is $\frac{\pi r^2}{r(h+r)}=\frac{\pi r}{h+r}$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{\pi r}{h+r}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-22.title: Work mod 3
amc12-ahsme-1979-22.body:
The left side is $m(m+1)(m+5)\equiv m(m+1)(m+2)\pmod 3$, a product of three consecutive integers, so it is divisible by $3$. The right side is $\equiv1\pmod3$. No solutions.

**Answer: (A) $0$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-22.title: Mod 3 table
amc12-ahsme-1979-22.body:
Mod $3$, $m^3+6m^2+5m\equiv m^3+2m$: for $m\equiv0,1,2$ this is $0,3\equiv0,12\equiv0$. The right side is always $1$. So there are $0$ pairs.

**Answer: (A) $0$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-23.title: Midpoints
amc12-ahsme-1979-23.body:
By symmetry the closest points are the midpoints $M$ of $AB$ and $N$ of $CD$: $MN$ is perpendicular to both edges. $CM=DM=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, so in isosceles $\triangle CMD$ the median $MN$ has $MN^2=\frac34-\frac14=\frac12$, $MN=\frac{\sqrt2}2$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-23.title: Cube
amc12-ahsme-1979-23.body:
A regular tetrahedron of edge $1$ sits in a cube of edge $\frac1{\sqrt2}$, with its edges as face diagonals. Opposite edges lie on opposite faces of the cube, so their distance is the cube's edge $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-24.title: Coordinates
amc12-ahsme-1979-24.body:
Put $B=(0,0)$, $C=(5,0)$ with $A,D$ above. $\cos B=-\frac35$, $\sin B=\frac45$: $A=4\left(-\frac35,\frac45\right)=\left(-\frac{12}5,\frac{16}5\right)$. $\sin C=\frac35$, $\cos C=-\frac45$: from $C$, $D$ is in direction $\left(\frac45,\frac35\right)$, so $D=(21,12)$. Then $AD^2=23.4^2+8.8^2=547.56+77.44=625$, $AD=25$.

**Answer: (E) $25$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-24.title: Drop perpendiculars
amc12-ahsme-1979-24.body:
From $\cos B=-\frac35$ and $\cos C=-\frac45$ (since $\sin C=\frac35$ and $C$ is obtuse), the angles $180^\circ-B$ and $180^\circ-C$ have cosines $\frac35$ and $\frac45$, so they are complementary. Extend $AB$ past $B$ and $DC$ past $C$ to meet at $E$: in $\triangle EBC$ the angles at $B$ and $C$ sum to $90^\circ$, so $\angle E=90^\circ$. With hypotenuse $BC=5$: $EB=5\cdot\frac35=3$ and $EC=5\cdot\frac45=4$. Then $EA=3+4=7$, $ED=4+20=24$, and $AD=\sqrt{7^2+24^2}=25$.

**Answer: (E) $25$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-25.title: Remainder theorem
amc12-ahsme-1979-25.body:
$r_1=\left(-\frac12\right)^8=\frac1{256}$, and $q_1(x)=\frac{x^8-\frac1{256}}{x+\frac12}=x^7-\frac12x^6+\frac14x^5-\dots-\frac1{128}$ (a geometric pattern: coefficient of $x^{7-k}$ is $\left(-\frac12\right)^k$). Then $r_2=q_1\left(-\frac12\right)=8\cdot\left(-\frac12\right)^7=-\frac{8}{128}=-\frac1{16}$ (each of the $8$ terms equals $\left(-\frac12\right)^7$).

**Answer: (B) $-\frac{1}{16}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-26.title: Step by one
amc12-ahsme-1979-26.body:
Set $y=1$: $f(x+1)=f(x)+x+2$. From $f(1)=1$: going up, $f(2)=4$, $f(3)=8$, ...; going down, $f(0)=-1$, $f(-1)=-2$, $f(-2)=-2$, $f(-3)=-1$, .... In general $f(n)=\frac{n^2+3n-2}{2}$ for integers $n$ (check: it satisfies $f(1)=1$ and the step rule). $f(n)=n$ gives $n^2+n-2=0$, so $n=1$ or $n=-2$. Exactly one integer $n\ne1$.

**Answer: (B) $1$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-26.title: Solve for $f$
amc12-ahsme-1979-26.body:
Setting $x=y=0$ gives $f(0)=-1$. Let $g(x)=f(x)-\frac{x^2}{2}+1$; then $g(x)+g(y)=g(x+y)$, so on integers $g(n)=ng(1)=n\cdot\frac32$. Hence $f(n)=\frac{n^2}2+\frac{3n}2-1$, and $f(n)=n$ iff $(n+2)(n-1)=0$. One integer besides $1$: $n=-2$.

**Answer: (B) $1$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-27.title: Count the good pairs
amc12-ahsme-1979-27.body:
There are $11^2=121$ pairs. Distinct positive roots need sum $-b>0$, product $c>0$, and $b^2>4c$. With $b<0$, $1\le c\le5$:
- $b=-1,-2$: $b^2\le4$, none.
- $b=-3$: $c<\frac94$: $c=1,2$ (2).
- $b=-4$: $c<4$: $c=1,2,3$ (3).
- $b=-5$: $c<\frac{25}4$: $c=1,\dots,5$ (5).

That is $10$ pairs, so the requested probability is $\frac{111}{121}$, not listed.

**Answer: (E) none of these**

amc12-ahsme-1979-28.title: Coordinates
amc12-ahsme-1979-28.body:
Let $B=(1,0)$, $C=(-1,0)$, $A=(0,\sqrt3)$. $C'$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, at distance $\sqrt{r^2-1}$ from the midpoint $\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$, on the side away from $C$, i.e. in direction $\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac12\right)$. So with $t=\sqrt{r^2-1}$, $C'=\left(\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2t,\frac{\sqrt3}2+\frac t2\right)$ and by symmetry $B'=\left(-\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}2t,\frac{\sqrt3}2+\frac t2\right)$. Then $B'C'=1+\sqrt3\,t=1+\sqrt{3(r^2-1)}$.

**Answer: (D) $1+\sqrt{3(r^2-1)}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-28.title: Check a special radius
amc12-ahsme-1979-28.body:
Take $r=\sqrt2$ in the coordinates above, so $\sqrt{r^2-1}=1$. Circles $A$ and $B$ meet where $|P-A|^2=|P-B|^2=2$; the outer solution is $C'=\left(\frac{1+\sqrt3}2,\frac{1+\sqrt3}2\right)$ (check: distance$^2$ to $B$ is $\left(\frac{\sqrt3-1}2\right)^2+\left(\frac{1+\sqrt3}2\right)^2=2$ ✓). By symmetry $B'C'=1+\sqrt3\approx2.73$. The choices give (A) $\approx2.24$, (B) $2$, (C) $\approx2.53$, (D) $1+\sqrt3$. Only (D) fits.

**Answer: (D) $1+\sqrt{3(r^2-1)}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-29.title: Difference of squares
amc12-ahsme-1979-29.body:
$x^6+\frac1{x^6}+2=\left(x^3+\frac1{x^3}\right)^2$, so the numerator is $\left(x+\frac1x\right)^6-\left(x^3+\frac1{x^3}\right)^2$. Dividing by the sum gives $f(x)=\left(x+\frac1x\right)^3-\left(x^3+\frac1{x^3}\right)=3\left(x+\frac1x\right)$. Since $x+\frac1x\ge2$ (equality at $x=1$), the minimum is $6$.

**Answer: (E) $6$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-30.title: Trigonometry
amc12-ahsme-1979-30.body:
In $\triangle CDE$, $\angle C=20^\circ$ and $\angle E=80^\circ$, so $\angle D=80^\circ$ and $CD=CE=\frac12BC$. By the law of sines with $AC=1$: $AB=\frac{\sin20^\circ}{\sin100^\circ}$ and $BC=\frac{\sin60^\circ}{\sin100^\circ}$.
- $[ABC]=\frac12\cdot AB\cdot AC\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sin20^\circ\sin60^\circ}{2\sin80^\circ}$.
- $\triangle CDE$ has $CD=CE=\frac{BC}2$ and apex angle $20^\circ$: $2[CDE]=CE^2\sin20^\circ=\frac{\sin^260^\circ\sin20^\circ}{4\sin^280^\circ}$.

Use $\sin20^\circ=2\sin10^\circ\cos10^\circ$ and $\sin80^\circ=\cos10^\circ$:
- $[ABC]=\sin60^\circ\sin10^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin10^\circ$.
- $2[CDE]=\frac34\cdot\frac{2\sin10^\circ\cos10^\circ}{4\cos^210^\circ}=\frac{3\sin10^\circ}{8\cos10^\circ}$.

We want to show the sum is $\frac{\sqrt3}8$, i.e. $4\sqrt3\sin10^\circ\cos10^\circ+3\sin10^\circ=\sqrt3\cos10^\circ$, i.e. $2\sqrt3\sin20^\circ=\sqrt3\cos10^\circ-3\sin10^\circ=2\sqrt3\left(\frac12\cos10^\circ-\frac{\sqrt3}2\sin10^\circ\right)=2\sqrt3\cos70^\circ$. Since $\cos70^\circ=\sin20^\circ$, this holds. So the total is $\frac{\sqrt3}8$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{8}$**

amc12-ahsme-1979-30.title: Numerical check
amc12-ahsme-1979-30.body:
With $\sin10^\circ\approx0.17365$ and $\cos10^\circ\approx0.98481$: $[ABC]=\frac{\sqrt3}2\sin10^\circ\approx0.15038$ and $2[CDE]=\frac{3\sin10^\circ}{8\cos10^\circ}\approx0.06613$. The sum $\approx0.21651$ matches $\frac{\sqrt3}8\approx0.21651$; the other choices are about $0.246$, $0.192$, $0.161$, $0.125$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{8}$**
